chapters.name: Chapter 1: Recognizing cyberbullying and responding safely

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What cyberbullying is (and is not)
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Tell cyberbullying apart from a normal disagreement.
This lesson builds toward: Given online situations, you will identify which are cyberbullying and which are normal conflict, explaining why using intent, repetition and power.
Cyberbullying is using technology to hurt, embarrass, threaten or target someone, usually more than once. Examples: mean or threatening messages, spreading rumors, posting embarrassing photos or videos, making fake accounts to mock someone, leaving someone out of a group chat on purpose to hurt them, or sharing private messages or images without permission.
It often happens through texts, social media, comments, direct messages, forums and games. Online posts can be permanent and public unless they are reported and removed, and they can spread to many people quickly.
Not every online argument is bullying. A one-time disagreement between equals is a conflict. Bullying is about hurting someone on purpose, often again and again, and often with a power difference: more people, more popularity, or private information to use against them. Some cyberbullying, like threats or harassment based on race, religion, gender, sexual orientation or disability, can be against the law.
Step by step:
- Ask: is this meant to hurt, embarrass or threaten?
- Ask: is it happening more than once, or spreading?
- Ask: is there a power difference (a group, popularity, private info)?
- If yes, treat it as cyberbullying and use the steps in this course.
Words to know:
- Cyberbullying: using phones, computers or games to hurt, embarrass, threaten or target someone.
- Harassment: repeated behavior that upsets, scares or threatens someone.
- Conflict: a disagreement between people; not the same as bullying.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Bullying
- StopBullying.gov: What Is Cyberbullying
Try it now: Read these three situations and label each one bullying or conflict: (1) a friend disagrees with your opinion about a game once; (2) a group keeps posting a fake account mocking a classmate; (3) someone keeps sending you threats after you said stop. Write why for each.
You can now recognize cyberbullying and tell it apart from a normal disagreement.

check.q: What usually makes something cyberbullying rather than a conflict?
options: It is meant to hurt, often repeated, and often with a power difference
Someone posts an opinion you dislike
A game ends in a loss
check.why: Bullying is about hurting someone on purpose, often again and again, often with a power difference.

check.q: A classmate is left out of a group chat on purpose, every week, to hurt them. How do you label it?
check.why: Leaving someone out on purpose to hurt them, again and again, is a form of cyberbullying.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Responding without making it worse
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Respond to a hurtful message by stepping away instead of fighting back.
This lesson builds toward: When someone sends you a hurtful message, you will step away instead of replying, fighting back or forwarding the post, naming three things you will not do and the next steps you will take.
When someone attacks you online, it is natural to want to hit back. But replying angrily, insulting them back or posting about them usually makes it worse, and it can make you look like part of the problem. KidsHealth advises not responding or retaliating, stepping away and not forwarding the message.
First, step away from the screen. Take a few slow breaths. Remind yourself: this is about their behavior, not your worth, and it is not your fault. Then follow the plan: save evidence, block, report and tell someone. You will learn each step in this course.
Do not forward or share the hurtful post, even to show friends how bad it is; that spreads it further. And do not pretend to be someone else or make fake accounts to get back at them.
Step by step:
- Don't reply or fight back.
- Step away and breathe.
- Remind yourself it's not your fault.
- Don't forward or share the post.
- Next: save evidence, block, report, tell an adult.
Words to know:
- Retaliate: to hurt someone back after they hurt you.
- Forward: to send a message or post on to other people.
Official sources:
- KidsHealth (Nemours): Cyberbullying (for teens)
Try it now: Someone comments "you're a joke, everyone hates you" under your post. Write what you will NOT do (three things) and what you WILL do in the next five minutes.
You can now stay calm, avoid fighting back or spreading it, and move to a safe plan.

check.q: Why is replying with insults a bad idea?
options: It usually makes it worse and can make you look like part of the problem
check.why: Fighting back usually makes things worse.

check.q: A hurtful post about you is going around. A friend asks you to forward it so they can see. What do you do?
options: Forward it to a few friends
Post it on your own page
Make a fake account to reply
Do not forward it; save evidence and follow your plan
check.why: Forwarding a hurtful post spreads it further.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Saving evidence
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take and store screenshots that prove what happened.
This lesson builds toward: When cyberbullying happens, you will save evidence with screenshots and a simple log before blocking anything, showing the username, date and time, and never saving or forwarding sexual images of a young person.
Evidence helps adults, schools, apps and police act. Before you block or delete anything, save proof. KidsHealth suggests screenshots or asking a parent to copy or save the messages.
A good screenshot shows: the message or post, the username or account name (and the profile page or link if you can), and the date and time. Save every incident, not just the worst one. Keep a simple log: date, app, what happened, who saw it. Store screenshots in a private folder or send them to a trusted adult.
One important exception: if someone sends or shares a sexual image of a young person, do NOT screenshot, save or forward the image itself; that can be illegal even for you. Save the username, the link and the messages around it, and tell a trusted adult right away. If someone is threatening to share sexual images unless you pay or send more, don't pay or send anything; block them but don't delete the messages, and get help. In the US, report it at report.cybertip.org, and use the free Take It Down service (takeitdown.ncmec.org) to help get images taken when you were under 18 removed.
Step by step:
- Before blocking, take a screenshot of each message or post.
- Make sure it shows the username, the date and the time.
- Save the profile link if you can.
- Write a short log: date, app, what happened.
- Store it privately or send it to a trusted adult.
Words to know:
- Evidence: proof of what happened, like screenshots and saved messages.
- Screenshot: a picture of what is on your screen.
- Sextortion: threatening to share someone's sexual images unless they pay or send more; it is a crime.
Official sources:
- KidsHealth (Nemours): Cyberbullying (for teens)
- NCMEC: Sextortion
- NCMEC: Take It Down
Try it now: Practice taking a screenshot on your phone of any harmless screen (like your weather app). Find where it saved. Make a private folder or album called "evidence" and write down the steps so you'll remember them.
You can now take screenshots that prove what happened, keep a log, and handle sexual images safely by telling an adult instead of saving them.

check.q: What is a good evidence log?
options: A list of date, app, what happened and who saw it
A copy of the bully's address
check.why: A simple log helps adults, schools, apps and police act.

check.q: You are about to block someone who sent threats. What do you do first?
options: Screenshot the messages showing the username, date and time
Forward them to the whole class
check.why: Save evidence before you block or delete anything.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Taking action and getting support

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Blocking and reporting on apps
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find and use the block and report options on the apps you use.
This lesson builds toward: On the two apps you use most, you will find the block and report options and check your privacy settings, without help.
Almost every social media app, messaging app and online game lets you block, mute and report. Blocking stops the person from contacting you or seeing your posts. Muting hides them without telling them. Reporting tells the company the person broke its rules; the company may remove posts or ban the account. KidsHealth also suggests reporting to your phone or email provider when bullying comes through them.
The options are usually found by tapping the three dots or the person's name or profile, or by pressing and holding the message. Menu names change, so if you can't find them, search the app's help or safety center for "block" and "report".
Also lock down your privacy: make your accounts private if you can, limit who can comment or message you, never share your passwords (even with friends), and think before you post personal details like your school, address or where you are right now.
Step by step:
- Save evidence first.
- Open the person's profile or the message, then the menu (often three dots).
- Choose Report and pick the reason that fits.
- Choose Block (or Mute if blocking would make things worse).
- Check your privacy settings: who can message, comment or see your posts.
Words to know:
- Block: stop someone from contacting you or seeing your posts.
- Report: tell the app or company that someone broke its rules.
- Privacy settings: choices that control who can see your posts and contact you.
Official sources:
- KidsHealth (Nemours): Cyberbullying (for teens)
Try it now: On the two apps you use most, find (but don't use) the block and report options for an account. Then check one privacy setting on each app, like who can message you, and change it if you want to.
You can now find and use block, mute and report on your apps and tighten your privacy settings.

options: Hides their posts without telling them
Lets them see more of your posts
check.why: Muting hides them without telling them; blocking stops them from contacting you.

check.q: Strangers keep commenting on your posts. Which privacy step helps most?
options: Share your password with a friend
Limit who can comment or message you
check.why: Limiting who can message or comment protects you.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Telling a trusted adult, the school and when to call police
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Tell a trusted adult what is happening and know when it goes to the school or police.
This lesson builds toward: When you or a friend is being bullied online, you will tell a trusted adult with your evidence and decide when it goes to the school or the police, naming two trusted adults and one person at school.
Many young people don't tell anyone because they worry it will make things worse, they'll lose their phone, or they feel ashamed. But adults can do things you can't: talk to the school, contact the app, or go to the police. KidsHealth says to speak up until you find someone who helps.
Trusted adults include a parent or guardian, another family member, a teacher, a school counselor, a coach, a mentor or a youth leader. Start simply: "Someone keeps sending me mean messages and I don't know what to do. Can you help? I saved screenshots." If the first adult doesn't help, tell another one. Most schools have anti-bullying policies, especially when it involves students; a school counselor or principal can act.
Go to the police, with an adult, when it involves threats of violence, sexual images or messages, photos or videos taken somewhere private (like a bathroom or locker room), stalking, or hate based on who you are. StopBullying.gov explains when to report to police and your state's bullying laws. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911 (or your country's emergency number). If the bullying leaves you feeling hopeless or thinking about hurting yourself, tell an adult now; in the US, call or text 988.
Step by step:
- Pick a trusted adult.
- Tell them what happened and show your evidence.
- Ask them to help contact the school if students are involved.
- Go to the police with an adult for threats, sexual images, stalking or hate.
- Danger now: call 911. Feeling hopeless: call or text 988.
Words to know:
- Trusted adult: a grown-up you feel safe with who can help, like a parent, teacher, counselor or coach.
- Stalking: repeatedly following, watching or contacting someone in a way that makes them afraid.
Official sources:
- StopBullying.gov: How to Report Cyberbullying
- StopBullying.gov: Laws, Policies and Regulations
- KidsHealth (Nemours): Cyberbullying (for teens)
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
Try it now: Write the names of two trusted adults and one person at school you could tell. Then write the exact two or three sentences you would say to start the conversation.
You can now tell a trusted adult with your evidence, involve the school, and know when it is a matter for the police or emergency help.

check.q: Which of these is a trusted adult?
options: A school counselor you feel safe with
A stranger online who offers help
check.why: Trusted adults include a parent or guardian, family member, teacher, counselor, coach, mentor or youth leader.

check.q: Someone sends you messages threatening to hurt you after school. What do you do?
options: Wait to see if it stops
Tell a trusted adult now and go to the police with them
check.why: Threats of violence go to the police, with an adult.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Being an upstander and making your safety plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Support someone who is being targeted and write your own safety plan.
This lesson builds toward: When someone else is being targeted, you will support them as an upstander and write your own safety plan, with every part of the plan included.
Most cyberbullying has an audience. A bystander watches. An upstander helps. You don't have to confront the bully in public to help; often the safest help is quiet.
Ways to be an upstander: don't like, share or comment on the hurtful post; report it; send the target a private message ("I saw that. It's not okay. Are you alright?"); invite them to hang out or sit with you; help them save evidence and tell a trusted adult. If you see threats or signs they may hurt themselves, tell an adult right away.
Now put everything together in your own plan, so you know exactly what to do if it happens to you or a friend.
Step by step:
- Don't like, share or comment on the post.
- Report it on the app.
- Message the target privately with support.
- Help them save evidence and tell a trusted adult.
- Write your own safety plan.
Words to know:
- Bystander: someone who sees bullying but does nothing.
- Upstander: someone who sees bullying and safely helps the person being targeted.
Try it now: Final task: write your cyberbullying safety plan: screenshot steps and where you'll keep them, where block and report are on your two main apps, two trusted adults and one person at school with what you'd say, when you'd go to the police, and one way you'd support a friend.
You can now support a friend who is being targeted and follow your own cyberbullying safety plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Saving evidence No screenshot steps, or no place to keep them. Screenshot steps that capture the username, date and time, and a private place to keep them. Also includes a simple log and the rule about never saving sexual images. Block and report Block and report options not found on the two main apps. Where block and report are on both apps, and one privacy setting checked. Also says when to mute instead of block. Who to tell No named adults, or nothing to say. Two trusted adults and one person at school, with the words to start the conversation. Also says what to do if the first adult does not help. When to go to police Missing or wrong. Threats, sexual images, stalking or hate go to the police with an adult; danger now means 911. Also names 988 for feeling hopeless and where to report online exploitation. Supporting a friend No upstander action, or the action spreads the post. One safe way to support a friend, such as a private message and helping them tell an adult. Two or more safe actions, including reporting the post. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is the difference between a bystander and an upstander?
options: A bystander watches; an upstander helps
check.why: Most cyberbullying has an audience; upstanders help the person targeted.

check.q: A friend's post says they feel like hurting themselves after being bullied. What do you do?
options: Tell a trusted adult right away
check.why: Signs someone may hurt themselves need an adult right away.
